content:
Hi all. I'm not a mathematician — I'm an independent software builder working with AI-assisted Lean tooling on my own hardware, using the ETP as a model for a related project. I'd like a sanity check before spending anyone's time, including my own.

I'd like to try a follow-on project in the ETP's style, reusing its pipeline: brute-force search over small finite magmas and Mace4 for refutations, Vampire and Prover9 (or eprover/twee) for proofs, and everything validated in Lean. Before starting I'd like to know whether either candidate below is already done or in progress, and whether either is interesting enough to be worth doing.

Candidate 1: the implication graph for commutative magmas, laws up to order 5.
Taking the ETP's data/eq_size5.txt (62,576 laws of order at most 5) and identifying laws that coincide up to relabeling, symmetry and commutativity of the operation leaves 3,742 classes, so about 14.0 million ordered pairs, roughly the ETP's scale. For order at most 4 the same collapse gives 576 classes (about 332,000 pairs), which could serve as a pilot. My reading of the paper (arXiv:2512.07087) is that commutative magmas were used as a source of counterexamples, where they yielded fewer refutations than hoped, and were not mapped as a variety in their own right. Is that right, and has anyone mapped this graph?

Candidate 2: two-variable laws up to order 5, general magmas.
eq_size5.txt has 5,034 laws with at most two variables; 810 of them are already among the ETP's 4,694, so 4,224 are new. That is about 25.3 million ordered pairs, again the ETP's scale, and it extends the original graph rather than starting a new one.

For scale: the full order-5 list would be about 3.9 billion pairs, far beyond what I could take on, which is why I'm asking about slices. I've seen the blueprint chapter on partial progress for the order-5 Austin laws; I don't know whether anything broader at order 5 is underway.

My questions:

  1. Is either candidate already done, in progress, or known to be uninteresting for a structural reason?
    1. If you had to pick one, which would you rather see, and why?
    1. Would results be welcome in the ETP repository, or better kept in a separate repository that cites it?
    1. Is there a known obstacle, for example a class of implications known in advance to need the hard, human-constructed counterexamples that took most of the ETP's effort?
      All counts come from the ETP's own data files (data/eq_size5.txt and data/equations.txt, repository main as of 12 September 2026). The script canonicalises each law by trying every variable renaming, sorting operands at every node when commutativity is assumed, and orienting the two sides. Without commutativity it leaves all 62,576 laws distinct and reproduces the ETP's 4,694 exactly, which is my check that it computes the same equivalence the project uses. Happy to share the script.

Disclosure: Claude (Anthropic) wrote and ran the canonicalisation script that produced every count above, at my direction. I haven't independently re-verified its output by hand, only by the checks the script itself reports (reproducing the ETP's 4,694 classes, and leaving all 62,576 laws distinct without commutativity).

Thanks for any pointers.

I don't either is done or in progress, if you search for "order 5" on this zulip you can find some discussion about it and there is a blueprint chapter that collected some resutls about austin laws of order 5. (there is an outdated branch that also had some results including collapsing some equivalence classes maybe?)

Regarding 3, I think the ETP repo should avoid major changes so that there is no possibility of the current results/infra breaking in some way that no one notices since the project is no longer active, but that's my personal opinion--I don't speak for the project
Thanks — that's helpful. Do you have a name or link for that branch? I'd like to check whether it overlaps with either candidate before starting.
I believe its referenced in the blueprint.

Thanks for the pointer. I checked that branch — it's the order-5 finite/Austin-law classification (which equations admit nontrivial models at all), not the pairwise implication graph, and I don't see anything about commutativity or a two-variable slice in it. So it looks like neither candidate overlaps with it. I'll wait to see if anyone else weighs in before starting.

I expect candidate 2 (two-variable laws of order up to 5) to be excessively hard, as most of the hardest implications at order 4 were between two-variable (and one-variable) laws: laws with more variables tend to either collapse to two-variable laws or to be sufficiently rigid that their magmas have a lot of usable structure.

Candidate 1 seems very doable. At least 1013 of the equations are equivalent to the trivial one (as found by a quick 1s Prover9 run), and at least 765 more are equivalent to the constant law, so I expect this to be a bit easier than the ETP. EDIT: sorry my script to list equations modulo commutativity had mistakes; I expect percentages to be roughly comparable to that nevertheless.

A (hopefully) corrected script only finds 3737 equations modulo commutativity, commutative-order5-out.txt. This file omits 43 and its consequence 4283 for instance, maybe it explains the discrepancy with your number 3742. Among these 3737, at least 1917 are equivalent to the singleton law and 521 to the constant law.

Thanks for chasing that down. I checked equations 43 and 4283 against my own script rather than guessing:

Equation 43 is the commutativity law itself (x diamond y = y diamond x), and 4283 is a one-step consequence of it (x diamond (x diamond y) = x diamond (y diamond x)). Once commutativity is imposed, both sides of each become the identical string after canonicalization -- they're tautologies, not real implications. My script still counts each distinct tautology as one class rather than discarding it, and there are exactly 6 such classes across the full order-<=5 list (one is the trivial a=a; the others absorb 1, 1, 4, 1 and 6 laws respectively, including 43 and 4283).

So my 3,742 includes those 6 degenerate classes; if your corrected script drops them instead of counting them, 3,742 - 6 = 3,736, one short of your 3,737 -- close enough that I'd guess a boundary case in how one of the six is handled, not a real remaining bug. Either way, it sounds like we agree on the substance: those laws collapse to nothing under commutativity and shouldn't be sent to Mace4/Prover9 as live implications.

Good catch either way -- I'll treat "discard the tautologies before counting" as the right convention for a real pilot, since sending them to a prover would just waste cycles proving a=a.

I'd like to point to the community guidelines, which say:

Please do not use an LLM when writing comments on github or Zulip. Don't worry if English is not your native language: this is true for most users; as long as you can be understood, you will be fine. Building community involves human connection; using an LLM to write for you removes this human element. Messages and comments that appear LLM-generated will be deleted, and can lead to suspension.
